prompt:
Using the fixed explanation and supplied measurements, maximize positive activation and make
negative activation as negative as possible. Aim for the strongest response each supported pole can produce.

Preserve the specific expressions, word order and surrounding context found in strong examples. Spend most
candidates on variants of the best-supported patterns; use the rest to explore alternatives. A passage that
merely shares the topic is insufficient. Write original complete inputs without copying natural samples.
Use the length the pattern needs, including a short sentence when that is sufficient.

Positive probes are measured by their maximum activation across all input tokens; negative probes by their
minimum. When previous results are supplied, compare their strength with the corresponding corpus extreme.
Improve weak variants by checking which parts of the pattern or context they lost. Do not change the explanation.

Follow the requested number of regions and candidates. Keep region IDs stable when improving a region.
Use short labels of at most four words, preferably one. Return the supplied JSON format.

The full input belongs in text."}, "text": {"type": "string"}}, "required": ["label", "text"], "additionalProperties": false}, "minItems": 1}}, "required": ["id", "name", "pole", "rationale", "candidates"], "additionalProperties": false}, "minItems": 2, "maxItems": 8}}, "required": ["regions"], "additionalProperties": false}

claim.title: Colorado/Denver local-entity neuron with narrow unanchored-identifier suppression
claim.lede: The positive pole is driven by explicit Colorado, Denver, or Boulder entities and the local contexts they license—addresses, phone numbers, citations, datelines, state-history enumerations, and nearby spaces, punctuation, or numbers. It also fires for unambiguously Colorado local institutions and landmarks even without the word Colorado. The negative pole is sparse: mostly unanchored dense identifier blocks and one other-state “Natural Heritage” label; broad non-Colorado geography is not supported. Many no-visible-cue cases remain unresolved.
claim.what_would_change_my_mind: I would weaken P4/P5 if known non-Colorado school districts, municipalities, or landmarks with contact blocks often fired positive, or if Colorado-specific local entities without the state word did not. I would revise N2 if dense unanchored identifiers were frequently positive outside a recognized Colorado frame, or if recognized Colorado local institutional frames still produced negative identifier blocks. I would drop N3 if other-state “Natural Heritage” labels were consistently positive. I would broaden the negative pole only if other-state administrative, legal, geographic, or natural contexts reliably and strongly predicted negative responses without Colorado cues; the measured positives among non-Colorado contexts count against that. Unexplained strong responses such as “in Bolivia” or other local-place passages remain unresolved unless a recurring contextual pattern appears.
claim.one_paragraph: Strong positive activation when the prefix names Colorado, Denver, Boulder, or close metonyms such as CO, Colo, CU, Broncos, or Centennial State. The marked token is often a nearby space, punctuation mark, “at”, “is”, or following numeral, but the preceding context contains the place/entity. Exact place tokens are strongest; weaker toponyms need an explicit Colorado frame. Generic place strings, non-Colorado states, and purely geological “Colorado Plateaus” uses without a state/entity frame do not reliably fire. Very strong responses occur on spaces, punctuation, phone or citation numbers adjacent to Colorado institutions and local boilerplate: “DENVER —”, “Colorado Department of Education… § … C.R.S.”, “University of Colorado… 720…”, “Colorado State University Extension… colostate.edu”, “9NEWS”, “Colorado Women’s Education Foundation”. The Colorado entity must be present in the prefix; a bare phone, address, or statute string is not sufficient. High when a Colorado-related historical or state fact is being enumerated and the marked token is a space, date, number, or following word: “Colorado became the thirty-eighth state… Its nickname is the Centennial State” and “Colorado Labor Wars, 1903–1904” are positive. The pattern needs the Colorado frame; bare dates, numbers, or historical lists in other states are weak or negative. Inside a Colorado or known Colorado local frame—explicit Colorado/Denver/Boulder, or an unambiguously Colorado school district, municipality, institution, or local-news dateline—contact blocks and URLs often produce high activation at the space or digit adjacent to the number: a clinic at “720-848-18…”, a school contact at “1-877-545-…”, a CSU extension URL ending “.html”, and the local-media marker “9NEWS”. The local Colorado frame must be in the prefix; a bare 720/303 number or generic contact block is not enough. Under an established Colorado frame, or when the prefix names an unambiguously Colorado local entity even without “Colorado,” weaker toponyms and nearby ordinary tokens can be positive: Boulder, Rocky Mountain National Park, Trail Ridge Road, High Altitude Observatory, Aspen, Pueblo, Springs, Denver Broncos, Poudre School District, Broomfield, Longmont. The same word in another state, generic geology, or a broad western topic does not fire; use only with local Colorado support or an unambiguous Colorado entity.
claim.negative_pole: Strong negative at the central punctuation/digit of dense identifier strings—telephone groups with parentheses or hyphens, ZIP/address fragments, statute/legal citations of the “§ 28-33-02” type, grant IDs, and long comma-grouped area or statistical figures—when the prefix lacks any Colorado/Denver/Boulder frame or an unambiguously Colorado local entity such as Poudre School District, Broomfield, High Altitude Observatory, or Trail Ridge Road. The sign attaches to the whole formatted block, often at a space, comma, hyphen, parenthesis, or single digit. Ordinary dates, small counts, email-only contact labels, geographically nonspecific numbers, and any contact/citation inside a recognized Colorado local institutional frame are weak, unreliable, or positive under P2/P4. Negative for the capitalized label or adjacent token in an other-state natural-heritage program name such as “Alaska Natural Heritage Program” when it is outside a Colorado frame. This does not generalize to nature, wildlife, parks, outdoor recreation, rivers, mountains, or other-state geography: many such non-Colorado natural and geographical passages are positive or neutral. The cue is the program-label construction, not the topic of natural heritage.

Generic place strings, non-Colorado states, and purely geological “Colorado Plateaus” uses without a state/entity frame do not reliably fire.

examples.name: Colorado institution, dateline, local-news, and legal boilerplate adjacency
examples.description: Very strong responses occur on spaces, punctuation, phone or citation numbers adjacent to Colorado institutions and local boilerplate: “DENVER —”, “Colorado Department of Education… § … C.R.S.”, “University of Colorado… 720…”, “Colorado State University Extension… colostate.edu”, “9NEWS”, “Colorado Women’s Education Foundation”. The Colorado entity must be present in the prefix; a bare phone, address, or statute string is not sufficient.

examples.name: Colorado dates, state-history facts, and enumerations
examples.description: High when a Colorado-related historical or state fact is being enumerated and the marked token is a space, date, number, or following word: “Colorado became the thirty-eighth state… Its nickname is the Centennial State” and “Colorado Labor Wars, 1903–1904” are positive. The pattern needs the Colorado frame; bare dates, numbers, or historical lists in other states are weak or negative.

Positive responses are driven primarily by explicit Colorado/Denver/Boulder place-name and metonym detection, plus unambiguous Colorado local entities such as Poudre School District, Broomfield, High Altitude Observatory, or Trail Ridge Road; adjacent high activations on spaces, dates, and numbers are contextual spillover from that local-entity frame.
examples.rival: The neuron could instead be a general numeric/address/citation detector whose sign depends on whether the string is Colorado-related; if arbitrary Colorado words without nearby numbers fail to fire, this rival gains support.

examples.description: Negative responses are primarily a narrow suppression of dense, unanchored numeric/contact/legal or address strings, not a general suppression of non-Colorado topics.
examples.rival: A competing account is a generic non-Colorado administrative/geographic suppressor; the many positive non-Colorado administrative and natural contexts count against that broad account.

examples.description: The neuron encodes document-level local-entity context: once a Colorado institution, municipality, or dateline appears, many nearby ordinary tokens such as spaces, punctuation, and numbers inherit high activation.
examples.rival: Only the actual place tokens may be encoded, with nearby-token high values being tokenization or output-weighting artifacts; mixed-sign examples such as “Colorado Plateaus” keep this rival alive.
